name: Astaroth
description: A Great Duke of Hell in Christian demonology, derived by demonisation from the Phoenician goddess Astarte / biblical Ashtoreth. Best known as Astaroth, ranked 29th in the Ars Goetia of the Lesser Key of Solomon, where he commands forty legions.
full_description: Astaroth is a major demon of Christian demonology. The name derives directly from the Hebrew Ashtoreth / Ashtaroth, the biblical name(s) for the West-Semitic goddess Astarte (Phoenician ʿAṯtart, Mesopotamian Ishtar), whose worship was condemned in the Hebrew Bible. Through the standard process of demonising the gods of rival pagan nations, this goddess was transformed by the early Christian period and the Middle Ages into a male demon. He appears in the Book of Abramelin (c. 1458), in Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1577) as 'a great and mighty duke' commanding forty legions, and as the 29th spirit of the Ars Goetia in the Lesser Key of Solomon, where he is described as 'a Mighty, Strong Duke' who 'appeareth in the Form of an hurtful Angel riding on an Infernal Beast like a Dragon, and carrying in his right hand a Viper'. He teaches the liberal sciences, answers questions about the past, present, and future, and gives the secrets of how the angels fell. In Sebastien Michaelis's hierarchy of demons (1612), Astaroth is a Prince of the Order of Thrones who tempts through laziness, vanity, and rationalised philosophies and whose adversary is St Bartholomew. In Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire Infernal (1818), he is depicted as 'a very ugly angel' riding a dragon-like beast.

regions: Christian Europe (medieval and early-modern grimoiric tradition)
origin: A textual phenomenon of Christian demonology and Western ceremonial magic, with antecedents in the ancient Near Eastern goddess Astarte and the biblical polemic against her cult.

etymology.origin: From the Hebrew Ashtoreth / Ashtaroth, denoting the West-Semitic goddess Astarte (Phoenician ʿAṯtart). The biblical Hebrew form was deliberately vocalised with the vowels of bōšeṯ ('shame') as a polemical device.
etymology.meaning: Originally the name of a Phoenician goddess of love, war, and fertility; demonised in Christian tradition.
etymology.first_use: Biblical Hebrew (1 Kings, 2 Kings, etc.); demonological use from the early Middle Ages; explicit demonic characterisation in Ælfric of Eynsham (d. 1010) and elaborated in 15th–17th c. grimoiric literature.

timeline.event: Ælfric of Eynsham (d. 1010) explicitly depicts Astaroth as a demon
Jacobus de Voragine includes Astaroth in the Golden Legend
timeline.significance: Wide medieval circulation of the figure

timeline.event: The Book of Abramelin (manuscript) treats Astaroth as one of the eight sub-princes
Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum lists Astaroth as a great duke commanding forty legions
Sebastien Michaelis publishes his demonological hierarchy, placing Astaroth as a Prince of the Order of Thrones
Urban Grandier's alleged diabolical pact (Loudun) includes Astaroth's signature
timeline.significance: Notorious historical case linking Astaroth to early-modern witch trials

timeline.event: Francis Barrett's The Magus reprints Astaroth's attributes
Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire Infernal popularises the modern image of Astaroth
S. L. MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley publish The Goetia (Lesser Key of Solomon)
timeline.significance: Standard modern grimoiric edition placing Astaroth as duke no. 29
